items.title: Oman rejects Iran's Hormuz toll plan in ceasefire dispute

featured_image.name: Oman rejects Iran's Hormuz toll demand. Can such fees be levied on ...

items.description: Iran's push to charge vessels up to $2 million each for transiting the Strait of Hormuz has become one of the most contentious elements of the two-week ceasefire agreed with the United States on Tuesday, drawing sharp opposition from Oman, Gulf states, and international legal experts who say the fees violate maritime law.

items.title: Vance calls Iran ceasefire 'fragile,' set to lead talks Friday

featured_image.name: US proposes replacing Witkoff with JD Vance on negotiating team ...

items.description:
US Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday described the newly struck ceasefire between the United States and Iran as a "fragile truce," urging Tehran to negotiate in good faith and warning that President Donald Trump is "not one to mess around."

Speaking at the Mathias Corvinus Collegium in Budapest during a two-day visit to Hungary, Vance said Trump is "impatient to make progress" and that Iran faces serious consequences if it does not engage sincerely in upcoming talks.[1][2]

"If the Iranians are willing in good faith to work with us, I think we can make an agreement," Vance said. But he cautioned: if Iran refuses to come to the negotiating table, "they're going to find out that the President of the United States is not one to mess around".[1]

items.title: NYT names Adam Back as likely Bitcoin creator Satoshi Nakamoto

featured_image.name: Adam Back Said It’s Still Early For The Retail Investors To Buy Bitcoin

items.description: The New York Times published an investigation on Wednesday naming British cryptographer Adam Back, 55, as the most likely person behind Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator Satoshi Nakamoto — a mystery that has persisted for 17 years since the cryptocurrency's launch. Back has repeatedly denied the claim.

items.title: IRGC takes de facto control of Iran as supreme leader reportedly incapacitated

featured_image.name: IRGC now de facto ruler of Iran, takes control of key state functions

items.description: Nearly six weeks after U.S. and Israeli forces launched Operation Epic Fury on February 28, Iran's clerical and political hierarchy lies in ruins — but the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has filled the vacuum, consolidating control over a country whose new Supreme Leader may be unable to govern at all.

items.title: Iran ceasefire reinforces view US emerged weakened, Bloomberg reports

featured_image.name: Trump Agrees to Ceasefire With Iran, Backs Off Threat of Sweeping ...

items.description: The two-week ceasefire between the United States and Iran, announced Tuesday evening just hours before a presidential deadline for devastating strikes, has done little to quiet a growing consensus among allies and adversaries alike: the roughly 40-day military campaign against Tehran has left America weaker on the world stage. Bloomberg reported Wednesday that the pause has "reinforced views among both adversaries and the NATO alliance" that the war marks a strategic setback for Washington, bolstering China and Russia while depleting American military and diplomatic capital.[1]

items.title: Hegseth declares US victory as Iran ceasefire takes effect

featured_image.name: Hegseth stampedes through the Pentagon - The Hill

items.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth held a Pentagon press briefing on Wednesday morning declaring what he called a "decisive military victory" against Iran, hours after President Donald Trump announced a two-week ceasefire that brought the 38-day Operation Epic Fury to a conditional halt.[1][2]

The briefing, delivered alongside Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan "Razin" Caine, came after Trump posted on Truth Social late Tuesday that the United States had "already met and exceeded all Military objectives" and agreed to suspend strikes on Iran for two weeks, provided Tehran immediately and fully reopens the Strait of Hormuz.[3][4]

items.title: Russia pushes three lunar missions to 2032-2036

featured_image.name: Russia Gets Bad News on Space Program As US Sends Artemis 2 ...

items.description: Russia has pushed back the launch of three lunar missions to the 2032–2036 timeframe, the Interfax news agency reported on Tuesday, dealing another blow to the country's space ambitions just as NASA astronauts completed a historic flyby of the moon aboard the Artemis II spacecraft.

items.title: SK Hynix jumps 15% as Samsung's record forecast lifts chip stocks

featured_image.name: SK Hynix shares jump 15% after peer Samsung projects blowout ...

items.description:
Shares of SK Hynix jumped 15% on Wednesday in Seoul, outpacing an 8.7% gain by Samsung Electronics and a 7% rise in the broader Kospi, after Samsung's preliminary first-quarter earnings guidance shattered expectations and signaled that the AI-driven memory chip boom is accelerating faster than anyone predicted.[1]

Samsung on Tuesday disclosed that it expects operating profit of approximately 57.2 trillion won ($37.9 billion) for the January-to-March quarter, according to the company's official earnings guidance. The figure represents a more than eightfold increase from 6.69 trillion won a year earlier and nearly triples the previous quarterly record of 20.07 trillion won set just three months prior. Revenue is projected at 133 trillion won, up roughly 68% year over year.[2][3][4]

items.title: IATA chief warns jet fuel recovery will take months despite ceasefire

featured_image.name: IATA chief says jet fuel supply could take months to recover after ...

items.description:
The head of the International Air Transport Association warned on Wednesday that global jet fuel supplies will take months to recover even if the Strait of Hormuz reopens, as damage to Middle East refining capacity continues to ripple through global aviation.

IATA Director General Willie Walsh, speaking to reporters in Singapore, said that the disruption caused by the closure of the strait since the U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran beginning February 28 has created a supply crisis that cannot be quickly reversed. "If it were to reopen and remain open, I think it will still take a period of months to get back to where supply needs to be, given the disruption to the refining capacity in the Middle East, which is a critical part of the global supply of refined products, and not just jet fuel for other products as well," Walsh said, according to Reuters.[1]

items.title: Starmer heads to Gulf to back US-Iran ceasefire

featured_image.name: UK PM Starmer in first Gulf visit to forge ties with UAE, Saudi

items.description:
British Prime Minister Keir Starmer is traveling to the Gulf on Wednesday to meet regional allies and push for the permanent reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, hours after the United States and Iran agreed to a two-week ceasefire that pulled the Middle East back from the brink of further escalation.[1][2]

"I welcome the ceasefire agreement reached overnight, which will provide a moment of relief to both the region and the global community," Starmer said in a statement before departing. "Together with our partners, we must exert every effort to support and maintain this ceasefire, transform it into a lasting agreement, and reopen the Strait of Hormuz."[2]

items.title: Oil plunges, stock futures surge after U.S.-Iran ceasefire

featured_image.name: Oil prices plunge below $100 after Iran agrees to safe passage through Strait of Hormuz during ceasefire

items.description: Oil prices plummeted below $100 a barrel and U.S. stock futures jumped on Tuesday evening after President Donald Trump announced a two-week ceasefire with Iran, pulling back from an 8 p.m. ET deadline that had threatened the destruction of Iranian civilian infrastructure. The announcement, made on Truth Social around 6:30 p.m. ET, marked a dramatic reversal from hours of escalating threats that had rattled global markets throughout the day.[1][2][3]

items.title: Amsterdam researchers build metamaterials that learn to change shape

featured_image.name: Shape-shifting worm blob model could inspire future robot swarms

items.description: Researchers at the University of Amsterdam have built synthetic materials that can learn to change shape, adapt their behavior, and move on their own — all without any central control system. The work, published on Monday in Nature Physics, blurs the line between engineered objects and living systems.[1][2]

items.title: China helped push Iran to accept ceasefire, AP reports

featured_image.name: China emerges as 'potential guarantor' in Iran-US talks amid Pakistan  diplomacy

items.description:
Hours before President Donald Trump's deadline for Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz expired on Tuesday, a two-week ceasefire was announced — and behind the scenes, China appears to have played a quiet but critical role in getting Tehran to the table.

According to the Associated Press, Chinese officials were in direct contact with their Iranian counterparts as ceasefire negotiations evolved, encouraging Tehran to find a path toward a deal. The New York Times reported that Iran faced pressure from China to accept Pakistan's two-week truce proposal, while the New York Post, citing Iranian officials, said China joined Pakistan in urging Iran to agree.[1][2][3][4][5]

items.title: Israel backs US-Iran ceasefire but excludes Lebanon fight

featured_image.name: Netanyahu orders military to expand invasion of southern Lebanon

items.description:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu endorsed President Donald Trump's decision to suspend airstrikes on Iran for two weeks, but made clear that the deal does not extend to Israel's military operations against Hezbollah in Lebanon, setting up a potential fault line in the fragile truce before negotiations have even begun.

The announcement came on Tuesday after Trump pulled back from his threat to destroy Iran's bridges, power plants, and civilian infrastructure, declaring a mutual ceasefire contingent on Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Israel agreed to the terms of the two-week ceasefire, according to the Associated Press, citing a White House official. But Netanyahu's office stressed that the agreement applies only to the Iran front — not to Lebanon, where Israeli forces have been conducting a grinding campaign against the Iranian-backed militant group since early March.[1][2][3]

items.title: Physical crude prices top 2008 records as Hormuz blockade deepens

featured_image.name: Tankers showing caution around Strait of Hormuz after attack on Iran

items.description: European and Asian refiners are paying record prices of nearly $150 a barrel for physical crude oil cargoes, surpassing levels last seen during the 2008 financial crisis, as Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz continues to choke global supply.

items.title: North Korea fires projectile a day after rare diplomatic thaw

featured_image.name: Suspected North Korean missile launch 'failed,' possibly ...

items.description:
North Korea launched an unidentified projectile from its capital area on Tuesday, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff confirmed on Wednesday, in a move that came just one day after South Korean President Lee Jae Myung expressed regret over drone incursions into the North.[1][2]

The JCS said it detected the launch from the Pyongyang region and that South Korean and U.S. intelligence authorities are analyzing the projectile, without providing further details. The projectile, believed to have been fired in the morning, apparently failed shortly after launch, according to the Korea Times, citing Yonhap.[3][1]

items.title: Physical crude hits all-time high as Hormuz crisis deepens

featured_image.name: Strait Of Hormuz Standoff Threatens Global Oil Supply - Grand Pinnacle  Tribune

items.description:
The price of physical crude oil surged to all-time highs on Tuesday, with some grades nearing $150 a barrel as European and Asian refiners scrambled for immediate supply, underscoring the severity of the energy crisis triggered by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

Dated Brent, the benchmark used to price much of the world's physical crude, reached a record $144.42 per barrel on Tuesday afternoon, surpassing levels seen during both the 2008 financial crisis and Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, according to data compiled by S&P Global Platts. North Sea Forties crude climbed to $146.09 a barrel, also an all-time high, according to LSEG data. When the Platts dated Brent assessment is used as a base, many physical cargoes effectively priced above $150 a barrel.[1][2][3][4][5]

items.title: US and Iran set for pivotal peace talks Friday in Islamabad

featured_image.name: US, Iran to pause war, agree to 2-week ceasefire

items.description:
Iran's Supreme National Security Council confirmed that formal negotiations with the United States will begin on Friday, April 10, in Islamabad, following a dramatic two-week ceasefire announced by President Donald Trump on Tuesday evening just 90 minutes before his own deadline to launch devastating strikes on Iranian infrastructure.[1][2][3]

The SNSC, in a statement posted to its Telegram channel, said Iran would enter the talks with "complete distrust of the American side" and stressed that agreeing to negotiate "does not mean the end of the war". Iran has allocated up to two weeks for the negotiations, with the possibility of extension by mutual agreement.[4][5]

items.title: Dated Brent surges to record $144 as Iran war chokes supply

featured_image.name: Dated Brent Oil Price Jumps to Highest Level on Record ...

items.description:
Physical oil prices hit an all-time high on Tuesday as the war in Iran, now in its sixth week, continues to choke global crude supply through the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Dated Brent, the benchmark for North Sea crude bought and sold for near-term delivery, soared above $144 a barrel — the highest level since the pricing series began in 1987, according to Bloomberg.[1][2]

The record in physical prices underscores the growing desperation among refiners scrambling to secure barrels for immediate delivery, even as Brent futures for June settled lower near $109 a barrel on Tuesday. The widening gap between spot and futures prices reflects a market where traders are paying steep premiums for crude they can get their hands on now.[1]

items.title: Oil prices drop as Pakistan-brokered ceasefire pauses US-Iran strikes

featured_image.name: U.S. oil price plunges 14% to below $100 after Trump agrees to two-week ceasefire in Iran war

items.description: Six weeks of war between the United States and Iran have sent oil prices soaring past $100 a barrel, fueling the sharpest inflation fears since 2023 and forcing the Federal Reserve into a holding pattern on interest rates. On Tuesday, a last-minute two-week ceasefire brokered by Pakistan offered a glimmer of relief — crude prices dropped sharply in evening trading — but economists warn the damage to consumer confidence and the inflation outlook may already be done.
